newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania and Hungary unveil monument to executed PM.
newsitem.headline: Romania and Hungary unveil monument to executed PM.

text.p: Romania and Hungary took a new step towards historic reconciliation on Monday, when they unveiled a monument to Imre Nagy, the executed Hungarian leader of a 1956 uprising against Soviet-dominated communist rule.

"The reconciliation between Romania and Hungary has turned into reality," Foreign Minister Adrian Severin told Reuters as Hungarian President Arpad Goncz and the mayor of the village of Snagov unveiled a marble obelisk erected to the memory of Nagy.
Nagy, a reform communist, became Hungary's prime minister during a 1956 revolt against Stalinist rule. The uprising demanded democratic freedom and national independence.

But after Soviet tanks rolled into Budapest in November 1956, Nagy was arrested and eventually taken to Romania and detained in a safe-house of the Securitate secret police in Snagov before being returned to Hungary and executed.

"This event is another step in this complex and difficult process," Severin said in reference to diplomatic efforts by Romania and Hungary, once uneasy neighbours, to end centuries-old rifts and pave the way to their early NATO admission.
Goncz arrived in Romania on Sunday for a "historic" visit, the first by a Hungarian head of state for 70 years.

"This obelisk is a symbol which prompts us to be united and to stretch out our hands to each other," Imre Mecs, a leader of the association of fighters in the 1956 revolt, told the crowd attending the ceremony on Monday.
Nagy was interrogated in Snagov by Hungarian police and KGB officials. He was hanged in Budapest in 1958, almost two years after the Soviet army had crushed the revolt.

Snagov resident Nicolae Tudorache, 78, told Reuters he still had vivid memories of the days when Nagy and his wife were held captives in Snagov and had occasional strolls along the shore of the lake bordering the village.
"She was a very beautiful woman. When allowed, they used to walk hand-in-hand, followed closely by Securitate agents. He always was the first to say 'Good day' when we met," he said.
"I felt very sorry for them. They were far away from their home and I knew how much they suffered. I couldn't stop crying when I heard that he had been killed," he said.

Ties between Romania and Hungary have been tainted until recently by what Hungary saw as Romania's poor treatment of its Hungarian minority of 1.6 million and by Romanian suspicion that Hungary still had territorial designs on Transylvania, which it lost after World War One.
Last year, the two states signed a political treaty which put an end to disputes and laid the ground for reconciliation.

Romania's new centrist government, which defeated the former leftist cabinet in last November's elections, entrusted the tourism portfolio and other junior ministerial posts to ethnic Hungarians, a first in post-communist Romania.
Romania hopes to be invited to join along with favourites Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic, when NATO announces its first eastward expansion at a Madrid summit in July.
